Complete excipient risk assessments for all approved excipients and assign risk classifications in accordance with the approved methodology.

A risk assessment should be implemented for higher-risk excipients associated with historical DEG/EG contamination incidents, such as glycerol, propylene glycol, macrogols below molecular weight 1000, and relevant polyol-based excipients. The assessment should consider factors including supply chain complexity, use of brokers or repackers, intended product use (particularly oral and paediatric formulations), supplier qualification status, existing supplier controls, and current incoming goods verification activities. The purpose should be to evaluate the current control strategy and define any additional controls required (e.g. additional testing).

A periodic verification testing program should be implemented for high-risk excipients to provide independent confirmation of supplier results. This does not necessarily need to be performed on every batch or container. A risk-based approach may be adopted, such as testing the first batch from a new supplier or manufacturer, annual verification testing, testing at defined batch intervals, or testing triggered by quality concerns or supply chain changes. Testing should include the relevant Ph. Eur. DEG/EG limit test performed by a suitably qualified laboratory.

Conduct a risk assessment to define the appropriate use and limitations of FTIR, Raman, and TruScan testing for raw material verification. The assessment should evaluate the suitability of these techniques for identity confirmation and whether they are appropriate for detecting impurities, such as DEG/EG. Where these techniques are not validated for impurity detection, the risk assessment should define what additional controls are required such as, supplier CoA review, periodic independent verification, or outsourced testing where required.

ES.SOP.066 should be updated to clearly distinguish between identity testing and impurity/contaminant testing requirements for higher-risk excipients associated with DEG/EG contamination risk. Based on the results of the risk assessment the procedure should define the purpose, capabilities, and limitations of FTIR, Raman, and TruScan testing and define which tests are considered appropriate for such contaminants.
The relevant PRSs should be updated to formally identify these materials and document the controls required to manage this risk associated with DEG/EG contamination risk.

Develop and implement a Raw Material Shelf-Life Assignment Risk Assessment Form to provide a documented scientific rationale for assignment of internal expiry or retest dates. The assessment should consider, where applicable:
•	Manufacturer expiry date 
•	Whether the material remains in the original unopened manufacturer packaging.
•	Frequency of opening and use.
•	Repackaging activities.
•	Exposure to air, moisture, oxygen or humidity.
•	Temperature sensitivity.
•	Photosensitivity.
•	Hygroscopicity.
•	Volatility.
•	Oxidation potential.
•	Microbiological susceptibility.
•	Physical stability considerations (e.g. crystallisation, caking, viscosity changes).
•	Chemical stability considerations.
•	Storage conditions.
•	Packaging type and closure integrity.
•	Available stability data, literature or pharmacopoeial information.
•	Historical use and quality performance within Eaststone.

The assessment should define whether the manufacturer's assigned shelf life can be retained, whether a reduced shelf life is required, or whether additional justification is necessary.

Update ES.SOP.066 to define the process for assignment of internal expiry and retest dates. The procedure should require documented justification for any deviation from the manufacturer's assigned expiry or retest period and prohibit use of a default fixed shelf-life assignment without supporting rationale.
